title: Brazil sets out why the first cut can precede the end of restrictive policy
summary: The minutes of Copom’s 27–28 January meeting, released on 3 February, explain how Brazil’s central bank could leave the Selic at 15.00% and envisage starting to cut at its next meeting. Policymakers had accumulated evidence that the existing level was suppressing demand and reducing inflation. Recognising the lag in that process warranted recalibrating the rate if the expected outlook materialised. All members still considered restraint necessary until inflation and expectations had durably converged. The document provides considerably more guidance about the possible start of the cycle than about its depth or duration: both would be determined as new evidence arrived (paragraphs 14–19).

The sectors slowing most were those most sensitive to financial conditions. Activity tied more directly to household income was proving more resilient. Copom interpreted this divergence as evidence consistent with transmission, while acknowledging that turning points produce mixed releases. Unemployment remained historically low, and average real earnings were growing faster than labour productivity. The Committee wanted to distinguish changes in the underlying structure of the labour market from the current position in the cycle, since these affect how employment gains pass into wages and ultimately sectoral prices. It did not conclude that the labour market had stopped posing an inflation risk. An investor seeking evidence of a sustainable easing cycle therefore needs to examine how the income-sensitive economy responds as well as the sectors where borrowing has already slowed (paragraphs 5–6).

Recent disinflation had spread beyond the headline index, but its sources differed. A stronger currency and more benign commodity prices reduced industrial-goods and food inflation. Services inflation also moderated, but more slowly, consistent with resilient labour demand and the gradual pace of aggregate deceleration. The Committee attributed part of the broader improvement to monetary restraint itself. Those observations fit together: favourable import costs can reduce headline inflation quickly while domestic restraint works more slowly on service prices. If that first channel fades before wage pressure eases, aggregate disinflation may overstate the scope for rate cuts. The minutes list a persistently more depreciated exchange rate and a more positive output gap among the relevant upside risks; a stronger domestic slowdown, trade-related global weakness and cheaper commodities are downside risks (paragraphs 9 and 12).

Survey expectations and the Committee’s projection give different readings of the remaining distance to target. The Focus survey put inflation at 4.0% for 2026 and 3.8% for 2027. Although measurements across different instruments and groups had declined, they remained above target at all horizons. In the Committee’s reference scenario, inflation accumulated over four quarters was 3.4% in 2026 and 3.2% at the policy horizon in the third quarter of 2027. The latter date is not equivalent to end-2027 in the Focus survey. Table 1 gives a different profile within the aggregate: market-determined prices move from 3.5% to 3.1% across these horizons, while administered prices move from 3.0% to 3.3%. Calculating a simple average of the two categories would discard their expenditure weights (paragraphs 3, 8 and 10–11; Table 1).

The projection is conditional on the Focus survey’s interest-rate path. Its exchange rate starts at BRL 5.35 per US dollar and subsequently evolves with purchasing-power parity. Footnote 2 describes the initial exchange rate as a rounded average from the ten trading days ending on the final day of the week before the meeting. Oil broadly follows its futures curve for six months and then rises 2% annually; the projection also assumes the yellow electricity tariff flag in December. Copom was still assessing the effect of extending the income-tax exemption. One should not interpret the 3.2% projection as the outcome of holding the Selic at 15% through the horizon, or the survey path as an official rate commitment.

Fiscal policy complicates the connection between an initial cut and the rest of the curve. Copom distinguishes near-term demand support from the longer-run effects of debt sustainability perceptions on the term premium. In its view, a weakening of structural reforms or fiscal discipline, more directed credit and uncertainty about stabilising debt could increase the economy’s neutral rate. A given nominal policy stance would then exert less restraint, raising the output cost of disinflation. The minutes report no observed change in the neutral rate or numerical estimate of the term premium. The conditional implication matters for positioning: the threshold for the first cut can be satisfied without establishing how far rates can fall, especially if the fiscal backdrop or inflation expectations deteriorate (paragraphs 7–8 and 14–18).

questions.question: Has the slowdown broadened from interest-sensitive activity into wages and service prices?
questions.detail: The minutes establish a sectoral divergence and real earnings growth above productivity, without identifying how much is cyclical. For the duration of an easing cycle, it matters whether employers are changing wage offers as demand slows. Compare activity and credit in rate-sensitive sectors with official labour income, productivity and service-price releases. Look for corroboration across several categories before treating an improvement in imported goods prices as evidence of domestic slack.

questions.question: How much of projected convergence survives less favourable exchange-rate or fiscal assumptions?
questions.detail: The starting exchange rate, oil path and tariff flag are explicit; the minutes provide no joint sensitivity to a weaker real and more persistent fiscal demand. A reliable sensitivity would help distinguish exposures to the first cut from the risk in longer-maturity rates. Consult central bank scenario analysis and contemporaneous fiscal accounts, and examine the household income response to the expanded tax exemption separately from changes in perceptions of debt sustainability.

questions.question: Which expectation measures indicate that anchoring is genuinely improving?
questions.detail: Copom sees declines across instruments and groups but still describes expectations as unanchored. A fall in the next year’s survey after cheaper food need not imply the same improvement at longer horizons. Compare successive Focus distributions at matched horizons with other expectation measures identified in the bank’s inflation publications, retaining differences in sampling and risk premia. Evidence of a persistent shift in the centre and dispersion would bear on the restriction required after the initial cut.
